@graph.headline: From technical founder to category voice: a 90-day profiling sprint
@graph.alternativeHeadline: A 90-day sprint to turn a technical founder into a category voice
@graph.description: A 6-minute founder profiling sprint: how to turn a technical founder into a category-defining voice in 90 days. Cadence, calendar, and the four hand-offs.

mainEntity.name: What is founder profiling and how is it different from press release PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Founder profiling is the deliberate, structured work of turning a technical founder into a category-defining voice across owned media (LinkedIn, X, podcasts) and earned media (op-eds, journalist interviews, conference talks). It is distinct from press release PR in three ways: the output is a person, not an announcement; the timeline is 90 to 180 days, not 7 to 14 days; and the success metric is whether journalists and AI engines start citing the founder by name when the category comes up, not whether a single launch was covered. Profiling makes every future press release land harder.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to build category voice for a Web3 or AI founder?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 90-day sprint produces the working foundation: positioning thesis locked, content cadence running, one anchor op-ed published, three to five podcast appearances done, LinkedIn and X cadence sustained. Real category voice — where journalists call the founder for quotes on adjacent stories without being pitched — typically takes 6 to 12 months of sustained work. Most founders compress this by tying profiling to a calendar moment (funding round, mainnet, product launch, conference keynote) where the visibility spike does 3 months of work in 6 weeks.

mainEntity.name: What are the four hand-offs in the founder profiling sprint?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hand-off 1 — positioning thesis: a single defensible point of view the founder will hold across every interview, op-ed, and panel. Hand-off 2 — owned-media cadence: a 12-week LinkedIn + X content calendar with the founder writing first-person posts, not ghostwritten polish. Hand-off 3 — earned-media stack: one anchor op-ed in a Tier-1 outlet, three to five podcast tour bookings, two conference panel placements. Hand-off 4 — journalist relationships: warm introductions to four to six beat reporters whose coverage arc matches the founder's positioning, set up for ongoing source-of-record conversations.

mainEntity.name: Do AI search engines cite individual founders or only their companies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, but with a meaningful structural difference. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews increasingly cite individual founders as sources when the founder has a documented track record of public opinions on a category. A founder who has authored op-eds, given podcast interviews, and been quoted in Tier-1 outlets becomes a citable entity in the AI engine's training and grounding sets. Without that document trail, the company gets cited but the founder does not — which means the founder's personal credibility never compounds. Princeton GEO research (Aggarwal et al., arXiv:2311.09735) shows named entities with quotation density attached drive a 30 to 40 percent uplift in generative engine citations.

mainEntity.name: Should I do founder profiling before or after a funding announcement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Before, when possible. A funding announcement is a forcing function: it puts the founder in front of reporters who would not otherwise take the meeting. If the positioning, content cadence, and op-ed pipeline are already running when the round closes, the funding announcement compounds. If they are not, the round generates a single news cycle and then silence. The 60-day window before a Series A close is the highest-leverage profiling sprint timing for any Web3 or AI founder.
